top_level_objectives: Describe the observed pattern of Mars’s apparent motion against the background stars before, during, and after retrograde motion.
Explain why retrograde motion occurs naturally in a heliocentric model when Earth overtakes Mars in its orbit.
Contrast the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric relative-motion explanation at an introductory level.
Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in terms of distance from the Sun and relative orbital motion.

scenes.scene_name: Nightly Sky Track: The Puzzle Appears
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce retrograde motion as an observational pattern seen from Earth, before explaining its cause.
key_visuals: A horizon-to-horizon night sky dome with fixed background constellations
Mars marked as a bright reddish point among labeled stars
A dated trail of Mars positions over many nights showing slow eastward drift, a westward loop, then resumed eastward motion
student_actions: Advance a night-by-night time slider through several months of observations.
Mark Mars’s position on selected dates and identify where its motion slows, reverses, and resumes.
Answer a prompt describing the pattern using the terms eastward, westward, and retrograde.

scenes.scene_name: Measuring the Loop Against the Stars
scenes.brief_purpose: Help students quantify the apparent loop and recognize that it is motion relative to distant background stars.
key_visuals: A zoomed star-field grid with right ascension-style east-west direction arrows
Mars’s retrograde path highlighted with date labels at station points
Constellation outlines remaining fixed behind the planet trail
student_actions: Use virtual measuring guides to compare Mars’s forward drift and backward loop length.
Identify the two stationary points where Mars changes apparent direction.
Explain why the background stars serve as the reference frame for apparent planetary motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show why retrograde motion was difficult to explain in an Earth-centered model and required added circular motions.
key_visuals: Earth fixed at the center of a simplified geocentric diagram
Mars moving on a small epicycle whose center moves around Earth on a larger circle
A projected sky trail showing the epicycle producing a backward loop
student_actions: Start and pause the geocentric animation to see when the epicycle makes Mars appear to reverse.
Compare the model’s constructed loop to the observed loop from the previous scene.
Reflect on why adding epicycles can reproduce the pattern but feels geometrically complicated.

scenes.scene_name: Outside the Solar System: Smooth Heliocentric Orbits
scenes.brief_purpose: Shift perspective to a top-down solar-system view where Earth and Mars move smoothly around the Sun.
key_visuals: Sun at the center with circular or slightly elliptical orbit paths for Earth and Mars
Earth on the faster inner orbit and Mars on the slower outer orbit
Date markers synchronized with the same retrograde event seen in the sky
student_actions: Run the orbital animation and observe Earth gaining on Mars.
Pause at matched dates and compare planet positions to the earlier sky observations.
State which planet moves faster and why the inner orbit matters.

scenes.scene_name: Line of Sight: Earth Overtakes Mars
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the heliocentric geometry to the apparent reversal seen from Earth.
key_visuals: A dynamic line-of-sight ray extending from Earth through Mars to a distant star background wall
Successive sightlines creating a projected path on the star background
Earth passing between the Sun and Mars near opposition
student_actions: Drag the time slider through the overtaking interval and watch the sightline sweep backward across the star background.
Identify the moment when Earth is closest to overtaking Mars and relate it to the middle of the retrograde loop.
Complete a short analogy prompt comparing the effect to passing a slower car.

scenes.scene_name: Perspective Switch: Same Event, Two Views
scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce that Mars does not physically reverse direction; the reversal is apparent and depends on viewpoint.
key_visuals: Split-screen view with Earth-sky star trail on one side and heliocentric orbit view on the other
Synchronized date cursor moving through both views
Color-coded segments for direct motion, stationary points, and retrograde motion
student_actions: Scrub through the event and match features of the sky loop to positions in the orbital view.
Select whether Mars ever reverses its orbital motion around the Sun and justify the answer.
Summarize the causal chain from faster Earth orbit to apparent backward motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the explanation to other outer planets and show why retrograde loops differ in size and duration.
key_visuals: Three projected sky trails for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn with comparable date scales
Top-down orbit diagram showing Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn at increasing distances
Relative loop sizes and angular shifts labeled for comparison
student_actions: Toggle between Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn retrograde events.
Compare which planet shows the most dramatic loop and which shows the smallest apparent reversal.
Explain how greater distance and slower relative angular change make Jupiter and Saturn’s loops less dramatic than Mars’s.

scenes.scene_name: Synthesis Challenge: Predict the Next Loop
scenes.brief_purpose: Assess whether students can apply the relative-motion model to predict and explain retrograde behavior.
key_visuals: Simplified heliocentric orbit setup with Earth and an unlabeled outer planet
Blank star background projection awaiting a predicted apparent path
Multiple-choice prediction cards for loop direction, timing, and relative size
student_actions: Advance Earth until it overtakes the outer planet and predict when retrograde will occur.
Sketch or choose the expected apparent path against the stars.
Submit a brief explanation of retrograde motion in one or two sentences.
